entries.title: Dream's slump gave the Sky a glimmer of hope on the Angel Reese trade
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — Angel Reese wants you to know she’s found exactly the home she was looking for.</p><p>Before facing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> on Sunday, Reese — recently named an All-Star for the third consecutive season — returned to a message she has repeated since Chicago traded her for two first-round draft picks.</p><p>“You can kind of see, honestly, this whole season I’ve been playing more free,” Reese said. “I don’t feel like I have a lot on my shoulders because they’ve helped me a lot — the coaches and everybody here with the organization.</p><p>“The sisterhood in the locker room has been amazing. It’s something that I really needed, so I’m really grateful for that. That’s why I wanted to come to Atlanta, for the sisterhood that I really needed in Year 3.”</p><p>That sisterhood got the better of the Sky on Sunday night, surviving a furious 18-point comeback and escaping with a buzzer-beating layup.</p><p>But the Dream’s season has not been quite as charmed as many expected.</p><p>And for a brief stretch, that offered the Sky some hope.</p><p>When the Sky traded Reese, it appeared the first-round picks they received from the Dream would land near the end of the draft. Those are the kinds of selections that often struggle to stick on WNBA rosters. The Sky, for example, selected Hailey Van Lith 11th in 2025, then cut her heading into this season.</p><p>That made the Angel Reese trade — which both sides described as mutual — look heavily lopsided against the Sky. Reese got her fresh start with a title contender. The Sky got picks that looked close to worthless.</p><p>Then came a twist.</p><p>The Dream hit a rough patch in June, struggling to shoot and, ironically enough, talking about many of the same problems as the Sky. They could not consistently put together a complete 40 minutes. They lost five consecutive games and fell as low as eighth in the standings.</p><p>Suddenly, the first-round pick headed to the Sky had some real value.</p><p>The Sky could use a middle-round selection to add a useful rotation player in the 2027 draft. Or the pick could become a more attractive trade asset for a team looking to move up — much like the Sky once did to acquire Reese.</p><p>None of those possibilities fully compensates for giving up a bona fide star like Reese. But they would certainly soften the blow.</p><p>The problem for the Sky is that the tide appears to be turning back in the Dream’s favor.</p><p>Atlanta recently got Brionna Jones back from injury, adding one of the league’s better post players and allowing Reese to spend more time at her natural position.</p><p>With their third consecutive victory Sunday, the Dream improved to 16-10 and moved into fifth place. Their slump might be over, with a clear path to climb back into the top four.</p><p>That would send the Sky’s return drifting back toward the bottom of the first round.</p><p>For the trade to look like anything other than a total dud, the Sky will have to make their post-Reese direction work.</p><p>Their second half comeback in Atlanta offered a glimpse of that possibility. Coach Tyler Marsh’s offense looked balanced, with five players scoring in double figures and contributions coming from throughout the rotation. Courtney Vandersloot — the veteran Reese once questioned as the centerpiece of the Sky’s plans — steered the fourth-quarter comeback with flashes of her younger self.</p><p>But once again, the Sky ended up on the wrong side of the final possession. They fell to 9-17 and remain 12th in the standings.</p><p>For now, no matter where the Dream’s draft pick lands, the scales remain heavily tilted toward Reese.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Balanced attack fuels Sky rally, but closing issues persist
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — What makes the Dream formidable is easy to identify and much harder to stop.</p><p>Before Sunday’s game, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> could point directly to the stat sheet. Atlanta entered No. 1 in transition scoring, second-chance points and points in the paint.</p><p>They turned the opening quarter into a live demonstration.</p><p>The Dream played at a blistering pace. All-Star <b>Rhyne</b> <b>Howard</b> knocked down wide-open three-pointers at one end and swatted away shots at the other. Atlanta crowded the Sky, rushing them into uncharacteristic turnovers.</p><p>By the time the Dream’s lead reached 18, the Sky appeared headed for a long night.</p><p>Instead, they turned it into one of their most exciting games of the season, rallying to take the lead in the fourth quarter.</p><p>“Offensively, we calmed down a little bit,” center <b>Elizabeth Williams</b> said. “We took care of the ball a little better, and defensively our intensity picked up. They were feeling really comfortable initially, and I think we took it on ourselves to turn that up.”</p><p>Ultimately, they lost on a last-second shot, another close game they could not finish.</p><p>But the way they fought back was encouraging. They disrupted Atlanta, generated stops and turned them into transition baskets. They shared the ball and settled into a smoother half-court flow.</p><p><b>Azurá Stevens</b> led the Sky with 20 points on 8-for-12 shooting. <b>Williams</b>, <b>Kamilla Cardoso</b>, <b>Sydney Taylor</b> and <b>Courtney Vandersloot</b> also scored in double figures.</p><p>That balance has come to define the Sky’s offense.</p><p>“Everybody eats,” <b>Natasha Cloud</b> told the Sun-Times. “That’s our philosophy. It is read and react while still giving us discipline with it. A lot of offenses will only focus on one or two people. Our offense, it literally needs everybody.”</p><p>Asked to rate the offense at this point in the season on a scale of one to 10, Cloud said she’s a tough critic and gave it a 7.5. She still sees too many lulls, especially late in games when every possession carries more weight.</p><h3><b>Huge shot</b></h3><p>Trailing by three with nine seconds remaining, the Sky called the rookie’s number. <b>Sydney Taylor</b> buried a difficult three-pointer to tie the game.</p><p>“Super proud of Syd,” Stevens said. “She plays with so much poise for a rookie and has so much confidence in herself. That play culminates who she is as a player. She’s not scared of the moment. It was a really, really tough shot.”</p><p>It was not Taylor’s first.</p><p>In her first start against the Liberty, she hit a three-pointer in the final seconds to put the Sky ahead. But, just as they did against the Liberty, the Sky followed her heroics by surrendering a wide-open layup. This time, Dream guard <b>Jordin Canada</b> slipped free for the winner at the buzzer.</p><h3><b>Cooling off</b></h3><p>Dream forward <b>Angel Reese</b> entered Sunday on a three-game heater but never found her rhythm against her former team.</p><p>She shot 3-for-13 before leaving in the third quarter with a lower-leg injury. Her efficiency struggles around the basket have continued in Atlanta, even as the rest of her game gives the Dream a boost.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Bipartisan housing bill is just one step toward expanding homeownership
entries.summary: <p>For generations, hard work and home ownership were supposed to go hand in hand. Yet for too many families today, the dream of owning a home — or even affording a stable place to rent — feels increasingly out of reach.</p><p>That is why the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/congress-road-to-housing-act-senate-21209cb780b76fe9a22881833c2dd535" target="_blank" >bipartisan passage</a> of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act is such a significant achievement. At a time when partisan divisions often paralyze Washington, lawmakers from both parties came together to confront one of the most pressing challenges facing American families: the shortage of affordable housing.</p><p>But Congress should view this legislation as a first step, not a destination.</p><p>America’s housing crisis is not simply a supply problem. It is an affordability problem, an equity problem and, increasingly, a wealth-building problem. Building more housing is essential. Yet if we stop there, we will leave millions of working families still locked out of the stability and opportunity that housing provides.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-370000" name="module-370000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Housing is more than shelter. Home ownership is the primary pathway many families use to build wealth, create financial security and pass opportunity from one generation to the next. When families cannot afford a home, cannot access fair financing or are displaced by rising costs, the consequences ripple through entire communities.</p><p>The challenges are particularly acute in Black communities and other historically marginalized neighborhoods, where decades of redlining, appraisal bias, discriminatory lending practices and unequal access to credit have limited opportunities for home ownership and wealth creation. The home ownership gap did not emerge by accident, and it will not disappear on its own.</p><h3></h3><p>That is why Congress must build on the foundation laid by the ROAD to Housing Act with a comprehensive national housing agenda that addresses both supply and affordability.</p><p>First, lawmakers should provide robust down-payment assistance for first-generation home buyers. For many families, especially those whose parents and grandparents were denied opportunities to accumulate housing wealth, saving for a down payment remains the single greatest obstacle to home ownership.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/4069" target="_blank" >Downpayment Toward Equity Act</a> and similar proposals would help level a playing field that has never been level. These measures would provide responsible support to qualified buyers while helping close persistent racial wealth gaps rooted in generations of exclusion from the housing market.</p><h3>Enforce fair housing laws</h3><p>Second, Congress must fully fund and vigorously enforce fair housing protections.</p><h3></h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/06/27/fair-housing-act-chicago-freedom-movement-discrimination-natalie-moore" >Fair Housing Act</a> remains one of the most important civil rights laws in American history. Yet laws are only as effective as their enforcement. Housing discrimination has not disappeared; it has simply evolved.</p><p>Federal programs that investigate discrimination, support victims and ensure compliance require sustained investment. Strong enforcement protects honest lenders, ethical landlords and responsible developers while ensuring families are judged by their ability to succeed rather than by their race, ethnicity or ZIP code.</p><p>Third, Congress should advance bipartisan measures that help families hold onto the homes they already own.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/1640" target="_blank" >Heirs Estate Inheritance Resolution and Succession Act</a> would help families resolve heirs’ property issues that often lead to involuntary loss of generational assets. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6125" target="_blank" >Housing Financial Literacy Act </a>would reward prospective home buyers who complete counseling programs, helping families make informed financial decisions and reducing the likelihood of future distress.</p><p>Similarly, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/5508" target="_blank" >Mortgage Insurance Freedom Act</a> would allow certain Federal Housing Administration borrowers who have built sufficient equity to stop paying unnecessary mortgage insurance premiums. That would put money back into household budgets — funds that could be used for savings, education, home improvements or small-business creation.</p><p>These proposals may not generate the headlines that large-scale housing legislation attracts, but they address real barriers that families encounter every day.</p><h3>Help people live in communities they serve</h3><h3></h3><p>Congress also should establish a recurring Housing Trust Fund supported by revenue accumulated through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. These resources should be dedicated exclusively to financing affordable and workforce housing across the nation.</p><p>The need could not be clearer. Teachers, nurses, firefighters, service workers and young professionals increasingly struggle to live in the communities they serve. Seniors on fixed incomes face mounting housing costs. Young families delay home ownership because prices continue to rise faster than wages.</p><p>No single policy will solve these challenges. But together, these reforms would create a housing agenda equal to the scale of the crisis.</p><p>The bipartisan vote on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act demonstrated Congress can still find common ground when Americans’ basic needs are at stake. Housing should be one of those issues.</p><p>Families need more homes. They also need a fair chance to afford them, finance them, insure them and remain in them. Housing policy should not simply increase the number of units on the market; it should expand opportunity, strengthen communities and create pathways to lasting economic security.</p><p>Last week, at the invitation of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., I joined members of the House Democrats’ Housing Affordability Working Group to discuss where Congress must go next. My message was simple: Increasing the housing supply is essential, but families also need policies that make housing truly affordable and accessible.</p><p></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-840000" name="module-840000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Driving home the point of medical safety
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://journals.lww.com/homehealthcarenurseonline/abstract/2007/10000/dangers_of_used_sharps_in_household_trash_.9.aspx" target="_blank" >Eight million people</a> in the U.S. use medical sharps — needles, scalpels, lancets — at home to manage conditions, such as diabetes, arthritis, allergies and autoimmune disorders. Disposing of these sharps properly is a critical, yet often overlooked, part of keeping patients and communities safe.</p><p>Recent studies highlight this gap in awareness. One <a class="Link" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5951232/#s4" target="_blank" >study</a> of patients with diabetes at an endocrinology clinic found that only 41% of participants disposed of their sharps correctly. Even in a healthcare setting where patients receive ongoing medical care, gaps in sharps disposal knowledge and practices remain widespread. Without clear guidance, Illinoisans managing conditions at home are left to figure it out on their own, increasing the likelihood sharps will end up where they shouldn't.</p><p>Fortunately, Illinois residents have access to clear disposal <a class="Link" href="https://myoldmeds.com/sharps/resources/illinois/" target="_blank" >guidance</a> and a wide range of convenient disposal options through <a class="Link" href="http://myoldmeds.com/" target="_blank" >MyOldMeds.com</a>, which is overseen by my organization, the Pharmaceutical Product Stewardship Work Group. The site offers a free, easy-to-use <a class="Link" href="https://myoldmeds.com/kiosk-locator/" target="_blank" >locator tool</a> that connects people to 75 safe sharps disposal sites across the state. Many of these locations are places people already visit regularly, such as pharmacies, grocery stores and medical clinics, making proper sharps disposal a practical part of everyday life.</p><p>When sharps are discarded improperly, the consequences can extend well beyond a single household. Needles placed loosely in trash bags, recycling bins or public spaces can create unnecessary hazards for sanitation workers who handle waste every day, and for children and pets who may accidentally come into contact with them. Safe disposal is not simply a matter of convenience; it is an important part of protecting communities and supporting public health.</p><p>I encourage Illinois residents to visit <a class="Link" href="http://myoldmeds.com/" target="_blank" >MyOldMeds.com</a> to learn more about proper sharps disposal and share these resources with their family members and friends. Together, we can make safe sharps disposal a routine part of responsible healthcare and community safety.</p><p><i>Irina Butler, executive director, Pharmaceutical Product Stewardship Work Group</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bb0000" name="module-bb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Nexstar-Tegna merger will protect local news</h3><p>Local journalism is more than a business — it is one of the most important institutions our communities depend on.</p><p>As someone who has dedicated his career to advocating for children, families and individuals with disabilities, I've seen firsthand how important trusted local journalism is to strong communities. Whether it's coverage of school board meetings, community programs or public safety updates, local broadcasters provide a public service that no algorithm can replace.</p><p>Local news helps families stay informed about the decisions that shape their daily lives. It shines a light on organizations serving our communities, connects people with vital resources and holds leaders accountable. For many nonprofits, it is also one of the most effective ways to reach volunteers, donors and families in need. Just as importantly, it gives a voice to organizations and individuals who might otherwise go unheard.</p><p>Today, however, local broadcasters are under tremendous pressure. As advertising dollars and audience attention continue to shift to global technology and streaming platforms, local news organizations face growing challenges in sustaining the journalism our communities rely on. Companies like Google, Meta, Amazon and Netflix command enormous audiences and advertising revenue, but they don't attend school board meetings, report on neighborhood issues or tell the stories of the people and organizations working every day to strengthen our communities.</p><p>That is why I support the proposed combination of <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/federal-judge-blocks-nexstar-tegna-merger-until-antitrust-lawsuit-is-resolved" target="_blank" >Nexstar Media Group and Tegna</a>. If local broadcasters are going to continue investing in strong local newsrooms and serving communities like ours, they need the scale and resources to compete in today's media landscape. The proposed merger represents a practical way to strengthen local journalism, invest in modern infrastructure and help ensure local stations can continue to provide the trusted reporting our communities depend on.</p><p>The future of local journalism should matter to all of us — not because of any one company, but because informed communities are stronger communities. Preserving local news means preserving accountability, civic engagement and a trusted source of information families rely on every day. For Chicago and communities across Illinois, supporting local broadcasters is ultimately an investment in the strength, safety and connectedness of the places we call home.</p><p><i>Dan Vosnos, Glenview</i></p><h3>Appreciating free-speech rights </h3><p>I recently read Alma Campos, Anna Savchenko and Keenan Chen's fine <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/10/asylum-russia-ukraine-war-tiulenev-immigration" >article in the Sun-Times </a>on the fate of dissidents to Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine. They are sometimes threatened for views contrary to those of Vladimir Putin, and finding refuge in our own country is becoming increasingly difficult. We need to be more appreciative of our right to free speech and should not take it for granted.</p><p><i>Thomas Dupre,</i> <i>Romeoville</i></p><h3>Amazing Aragon memories</h3><p>When I was a young college student in the late 1950s, I had a job at the parking lot adjacent to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/07/15/aragon-ballroom-100-years-uptown" >Aragon Ballroom</a>, which is celebrating 100 years. It was in the pre-concert days. What I remember most is the joy and cheerfulness of the singles and couples who came for a night of dancing and entertainment. The men wore suits and ties, and the ladies wore dresses. You could see that they had optimistic anticipation of what the evening might bring. The Aragon was the place.</p><p><i>Philip S. Witt, Northbrook</i></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Visits to husband's grandkids have lost their appeal
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm 56 years old and have been married for 12 years. I don't want to drive an hour and a half to spend time with my husband's grandbabies. I have done that on many occasions and choose not to do it anymore. I'm not into babies — or children, for that matter. He continues to ask me to go and can't understand why I don't want to. I have no problem with him going (I encourage him to go), but he won't let up on me, and it's driving me away. Am I wrong to prefer not to go? — <i>CHILD-FREE IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR CHILD-FREE:</b> Has it occurred to you that your husband may not want to drive an hour and a half to visit the "grandbabies" any more than you do? He may need you for backup. Sometimes in a marriage, we do things for our partner that may not be our favorite pastime, but we do it for love. You should not have to make that pilgrimage every time your husband does, but the nice thing to do would be to accompany him more times than not. And do it with a smile.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband is serving a life sentence, with the possibility of parole. He turned himself in a year and a half ago for a crime that happened 15 years ago.</p><p>I met someone seven months ago. This man is involved in his church and has a ministry in which he feeds the homeless. I'm not sure at this point what our future holds. I feel so guilty at times. Please help. Any advice would be greatly appreciated. — <i>CONFLICTED IN GEORGIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR CONFLICTED:</b> This is something I think you should discuss with your incarcerated husband. When you do, explain that you don't think you can live like a widow, possibly for decades. Decide together how you should proceed. However, please remember you have been involved with this new person for a relatively short time, and there is no guarantee that your relationship will become permanent.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Our friend "Leo" married a girl who treats him poorly. She degrades him in front of people about his finances, weight, looks, etc. They have been married only a couple of years and have no kids. Leo is a great person, and his mental health is getting beaten down daily. Should we say something to him? We want him to know we would support him if he wanted to divorce her. He has limited family — his friends are family. — <i>STEPPING UP IN IDAHO</i></p><p><b>DEAR STEPPING UP:</b> Because you and Leo's other friends believe he is being abused, I see no reason to remain silent and pretend it isn't happening. An intervention may be called for, as well as an opportunity to reinforce the message that you are all there for him regardless of what he chooses to do about his marriage.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Abby shares more than 100 of her favorite recipes in two booklets: "Abby's Favorite Recipes" and "More Favorite Recipes by Dear Abby." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $16 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Cookbooklet Set, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Chicago cabbies and ride-hailing drivers are both struggling amid changing industry: 'I'm stuck in this'
entries.summary: <p>The way Bob Singh sees it, the taxi industry has drastically changed, but he and other cabbies are still playing by the old rules, struggling to stay afloat as ride-hailing companies like Uber and Lyft dominate the market.</p><p>“Financially, it’s devastating,” Singh, 57, said.</p><p>But in the last few years, ride-hailing drivers have hit their own speed bumps. The app-based companies control their fares and the trips available to them, take an ever-changing percentage of their pay and sometimes cut off drivers’ accounts at a moment’s notice. City and state lawmakers recently took steps to support both cabbies and ride-hailing drivers but some worry it may be too little too late.</p><p>Since the pandemic, major commuting pattern shifts have hurt both taxis and ride-hailing services. And then there’s the emerging threat <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/02/25/waymo-autonomous-vehicle-robotaxi-buckner-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>of autonomous vehicles</u></a> looming over both.</p><p>Still, cab drivers have had the roughest road to navigate as the industry evolves. The competition from ride-hailing apps has sharply reduced the demand for cabs and therefore the value of taxi medallions — the government-issued permit required for taxis. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7d0000" name="html-embed-module-7d0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/29662421"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/29662421/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In Chicago, the price of a taxi medallion peaked in 2012 at nearly $400,000, according to city data. Now, they go for around $5,000, which has left many Chicago cabbies in significant debt. </p><p>A taxi driver for 36 years, Singh said he feels “stuck” in the business. He was just a kid when his family moved from India to the U.S., and he started driving taxis at 21.</p><p>Singh bought his first medallion in 1991 for $20,000. Two decades later, when he and his brother bought another medallion, it was valued at $360,000. But as the market for those medallions has plummeted, they still owe around $490,000 on the loan, with a monthly payment of nearly $3,500.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div It was not easy, but, I mean, what can you do?”</p><p>On a typical day, Singh makes about $80 from six rides, though he’s scaled back his driving in recent years to focus on managing his other vehicles and spending more time with family. Based on conversations with the drivers he works with, he estimated that the average Chicago taxi driver makes around $20 per hour, if not less. An exact citywide average is not publicly available. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/c1F4j_DSZz0?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Can Chicago save its taxis? The fight to keep the meter running."></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>‘An albatross around the neck of the taxicab industry’</h3><p>When the recent fare hike was being considered, some speculated <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/04/16/chicago-cabbies-conflicted-about-fare-hike-intended-to-save-dying-taxi-industry" >it might reduce cab ridership</a>. But a couple weeks after Chicago's first taxi fare increase since 2016 took, Singh said his drivers "are happy."</p><p>"So far, I think it's a positive step," Singh said.</p><p>Cab drivers say the 20% fare increase was long overdue to help them keep up with ride-hailing competition and skyrocketing costs.</p><p>“Will this increase help? app-based services.</p><p>As of May, about 85,000 ride-hailing drivers were registered in Chicago, according to city data. That compares with about 2,600 active taxi licenses in the city.</p><p>Nearly a decade ago, in 2017, there were almost 25 million total taxi rides in the city. But as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/news/2014/06/05/rideshare-vs-taxicabs-the-inside-story" target="_blank" >ride-hailing companies gained a foothold</a> in Chicago, the market was upended.</p><p>In November and December 2018, the first two months of available ride-hailing data, the companies racked up 17.5 million rides, almost as many rides as cabs had that entire year. The following year, ride-hailing riders made nearly 112 million trips, the most ever. Meanwhile, taxi ridership dropped 21%.</p><p>Fast forward to this year. On an average day in May, Chicago riders took about 22,000 cab rides — but about 250,000 ride-hailing trips. with its own set of challenges.</p><p>While the barriers to entry are lower than the taxi industry, many ride-hailing drivers find themselves earning modest incomes while remaining heavily dependent on platforms that dictate the terms of their work.</p><p>That led to a push by ride-hailing drivers to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/06/04/illinois-general-assembly-bill-rideshare-uber-lyft-drivers-unionize" target="_blank" ><u>pass a state law in May</u></a> allowing them to form unions. The bill awaits Gov. JB Pritzker’s signature.</p><p>“Because affordability is at the top of everyone’s mind with gas prices rising, drivers really can’t wait. They are scraping by right now,” said Bailey Koch, spokesperson for the Illinois Drivers Alliance. “This is their full-time job, it’s how they pay their bills and they just cannot keep up. And there’s absolutely no way they can make a change in their workplace without forming a union.”</p><p>In a statement, a spokesperson for Uber said the company supports the state law "because it preserves the flexibility that drivers consistently tell us they value most while creating a statewide framework for benefits, representation, and workplace protections."</p><p>A spokesperson for Lyft said the company looks forward to "working collaboratively" on the bill's implementations and "addressing some of the rider impact concerns we have during rule making later this year."</p><div Ride-hailing companies take a cut, but the exact percentage can vary and is not disclosed. A spokesperson for Uber said, "A significant and growing portion of the fare goes toward covering insurance costs."</p><p>Lyft takes about 14% of what passengers pay for a ride, and the company caps that share at 30%, according to a company spokesperson. After Lyft takes its share, then an undisclosed amount goes toward insurance, taxes and government-mandated fees, the driver takes home the rest.</p><p>“Unfortunately, there is not a real breakdown of [pay],” Koch said. “That is, I think, what’s really frustrating because there’s no transparent reason as to why a ride is a certain amount of money. they’re just stuck.”</p><h3><b>‘What am I going to do?’</b></h3><p>For the taxi industry to survive and coexist with ride-hailing services, legal reforms for cabbies and more regulations for in Illinois, the future is just as uncertain but a little less gloomy.</p><p>Forming a union could help rebalance their relationship with ride-hailing companies. And it might provide some protections from the growing autonomous vehicle industry led by companies like Waymo.</p><p>“In the same way that the Uber and Lyft drivers have taken away from cab drivers, those [autonomous vehicles] are trying to take away from us again,” Echevarria said. “So imagine in one generation being a cab driver that then has had your job taken away [by] Uber and then you become an Uber driver, and then you have your job taken away [by] Waymo.” </p><p><i>Contributing: Cam Rodriguez</i></p>

entries.title: St. Vincent explores ‘new dimension’ in orchestra collabs
entries.summary: <p>Musician Annie Clark, the multi-instrumentalist who performs under the name St. Vincent, is no stranger to reinvention.  </p><p>Much like her creative heroes — David Bowie, Prince, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/02/05/david-byrne-chicago-theater-of-the-mind-goodman-talking-heads" target="_blank" ><u>David Byrne</u></a> — Clark’s sound and stage presence have evolved throughout the nearly 20 years since her debut album, “Marry Me,” was released in 2007. Now Clark continues to defy genres by appearing with a full orchestra, including a performance with the <a class="Link" href="https://www.ravinia.org/events/detail/st-vincent-cso-260725" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Symphony Orchestra this weekend at Ravinia</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>“Every night, really, truly is such an endorphin boost,” said the 43-year-old Clark, who splits her time between New York (which she calls “my heart’s home”), Los Angeles and her native Texas.</p><p>The “St. Vincent Live With Orchestra” project debuted last fall at London’s Royal Albert Hall as part of the longstanding BBC Proms series and was released as a live album in March. The reimagined versions of songs from across Clark’s catalog — including “Paris is Burning” and “Smoking Section” — were brought to life in collaboration with the composer and arranger Jules Buckley, whom Clark was introduced to through her longtime friend and keyboardist Rachel Eckroth.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.ravinia.org/events/detail/st-vincent-cso-260725" target="_blank" ><b><u>St. Vincent with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra</u></b></a></h3>6 p.m., Saturday, July 25<br>Ravinia Hunter Pavilion<br>Tickets from $55</div> </div><p>This summer, Clark, Buckley and a small band of players — including Eckroth — have taken the show on the road for a tour with local orchestras that began in Pittsburgh in June, wound through Boston and New York, and will come to the Chicago suburbs before concluding in August at the Hollywood Bowl.</p><p>The project gave Clark a chance to dig through her archive for songs ripe for orchestral rearrangement and spotlight some of her lesser-known early work, which she says was inspired by composers like Igor Stravinsky.</p><p>“It all kind of started [by] going ‘all right, which songs in the catalog are going to be made better, cooler with a new dimension with the symphony?’” Clark said. “I definitely wanted to honor some of the songs from the earlier records that I haven't touched in a really long time and give them their flowers.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-750000" name="image-750000"></a> <picture Here, she performs at Riot Fest in 2024. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>When we spoke in mid-June, Clark was in New York between tour dates. During the interview for this story, Clark was walking around the city when a man stopped her and asked for money. After she sweetly told him she didn’t have any cash on her, she ducked into a bodega, offering to buy him the pizza and Hawaiian punch he selected. “I got you, baby,” she said.</p><p>Back outside, she said into the phone, “There's this kid, you know, he's strung out. He needed something.”</p><p>And then, seamlessly, she dove back into talking about her music. “In this weird way, this concert became kind of like — I'm not nearly dead, thank God — but it became sort of a midlife career retrospective,” she said.</p><p>While the orchestral project is a totally new endeavor for the six-time Grammy-Award-winning Clark, it puts her in the company of many pop peers, who have also recently waded into the world of classical collaborations.</p><p>There's Rosalía, whose latest album, “Lux,” was recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra. And in Chicago this summer, <a class="Link" href="https://chicagophilharmonic.org/events/lucy-dacus/?l=L1&ri=0" target="_blank" ><u>Lucy Dacus</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.grantparkmusicfestival.com/events/an-evening-with-ben-folds/" target="_blank" ><u>Ben Folds</u></a> are among the rock singers appearing with the Chicago Philharmonic and Grant Park Orchestra, respectively, while <a class="Link" href="https://www.ravinia.org/events/detail/hunter-pavilion-cso-90-opening-260711" target="_blank" ><u>Lizzo</u></a> and her flute helped kick off CSO’s season at Ravinia, and hometown artist <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/02/24/andrew-bird-debut-chicago-symphony-orchestra" target="_blank" ><u>Andrew Bird</u></a> will appear with the orchestra this fall.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d50000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Lizzo is another artist collaborating with a Chicago orchestra this summer. Here, she Lizzo performs Giulio Briccialdi’s “Carnival of Venice” with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra on the opening night of Ravinia Festival.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Another prominent local example of rock-orchestra collaborations was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/11/18/billy-corgan-smashing-pumpkins-night-of-mellon-collie-infinite-sadness-lyric-opera" target="_blank" ><u>Billy Corgan</u></a>’s reimagination of the Smashing Pumpkins’ hit album “Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness.” Last fall, he debuted the project, backed by the Lyric Opera’s full orchestra and chorus, in a sold-out run of seven shows.</p><p>In the Corgan project, the songs were reimagined solely as symphonic works, without guitar or drum parts. In the St. Vincent universe, Clark does retain the role of world-class guitar shredder (Rolling Stone named <a class="Link" href="https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-guitarists-1234814010/st-vincent-19-1234814295/" target="_blank" ><u>Clark the 26th greatest guitarist of all time</u></a>). She is joined onstage by her touring guitarist, bassist, drummer and keyboardist, in addition to the members of the orchestra.</p><p>While the trend of popular-star-goes-classical seems to be everywhere, it’s hardly new. In 1999, Metallica brought their heavy metal sound to a collaboration with the San Francisco Symphony on a series of live shows that resulted in the five-time platinum album “S&M.”</p><p>Still, the need for these types of crossover programs seems more urgent, as arts administrators in the classical universe look to attract broader audiences in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>CSO bassist Dan Carson said he understands the need to fill out a season with shows that have broad, mainstream appeal. When we spoke, Carson and his colleagues were fresh off their final shows at Symphony Center for the season: A three-night run of “Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back,” in which the orchestra played John Williams’ score live.</p><p>He knows that these types of events, whether Downtown or at Ravinia, are a way to sell tickets. And while he said, “We obviously love Mozart and Mahler,” he also said there’s something about the buzz of a sold-out audience — dressed up as Princess Leia or Stormtroopers — that is infectious. “I want people to go nuts,” Carson said. “I really like the energy.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b40000" name="image-b40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f90ede7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+130/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe0%2Fdea2b0db4566945357921d60efd4%2Flollasat-080418-8.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cae5241/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+130/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe0%2Fdea2b0db4566945357921d60efd4%2Flollasat-080418-8.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9ed7e83/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+130/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe0%2Fdea2b0db4566945357921d60efd4%2Flollasat-080418-8.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="St. Vincent performs at Lollapalooza in 2018. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9ed7e83/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+130/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe0%2Fdea2b0db4566945357921d60efd4%2Flollasat-080418-8.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/952312c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+130/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe0%2Fdea2b0db4566945357921d60efd4%2Flollasat-080418-8.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9ed7e83/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+130/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe0%2Fdea2b0db4566945357921d60efd4%2Flollasat-080418-8.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Clark said that when she arrives in a new city, she likes “the process of slowly winning orchestras over,” but there’s typically only one rehearsal to do it.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And when artists of other genres — whether jazz singer <a class="Link" href="https://cso.org/about/performers/visiting-artists/vocals/samara-joy/" target="_blank" ><u>Samara Joy</u></a> or bluegrass-rooted <a class="Link" href="https://cso.org/performances/25-26/scp-featured-concerts/an-evening-with-chris-thile/" target="_blank" ><u>Chris Thile</u></a> — come to town, Carson said there’s generally a mutual respect. Though he said sometimes the music retrofitted for orchestral players isn’t so challenging.</p><p>“Something that's common is that they'll have an electric bass player, so having the orchestral bass in addition to that is almost a little bit redundant,” Carson said, “so we'll just kind of add some maybe pizzicato, some plucking to give it some texture or something.”</p><p>Clark said that when she arrives in a new city, she likes “the process of slowly winning orchestras over,” but there’s typically only one rehearsal to do it.</p><p>“I like seeing them transition from ‘Oh man, when's this going to be over?’ to ‘We had a good time with nice, talented people, and we enjoyed that.’”</p><p>For Clark, the way to do that is by being respectful; plus, she said, “The charts are really good.”</p><p>“It's so beautiful. I mean, 60 incredible musicians playing music conducted by a great conductor,” Clark said. “When do 60 people come together to do anything? I just get to bathe in beauty.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ. </i></p>

entries.title: Illinois Republican Party chair Bob Grogan aims to shake off 'Stockholm syndrome' of struggling state GOP
entries.summary: <p>It doesn’t take a professional auditor to conclude the Illinois Republican Party is stuck in a rut, but the state GOP is hoping one can get them back on the path to relevance.</p><p>Nearly 12 years removed from their last statewide election victory and long relegated to super-minority status in Springfield, Republicans have tapped former DuPage County Auditor Bob Grogan to chair the state party, aiming to revitalize the suburban base that has largely abandoned the GOP under President Donald Trump.</p><p>Grogan spent 12 years as an elected watchdog keeping tabs on various arms of the county government, and he has no misconceptions about his new volunteer post recruiting candidates, fundraising and, most importantly, attempting to unite a fractured party.</p><p>“You get blamed for everything and credit for nothing,” Grogan told the Sun-Times. “I'm not in it for the glory. I like to say professionally, what I do is I fix broken things. And that's my audit background, where you find problems, and you don't play ‘gotcha.’ You just say, ‘Here’s a list of solutions. Let's try to go out and do it.’”</p><p>He’ll need a long list in the wake of his predecessor, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/07/12/kathy-salvi-illinois-republican-party-chair" target="_blank" ><u>Kathy Salvi</u></a>, who wasn’t able to make many statewide inroads before Grogan unseated her in a May vote by the Republican State Central Committee.</p><p>“She was more aspirational, and I'm more operational,” said Grogan, who doesn’t embrace Trump quite as enthusiastically as Salvi did. Grogan compared the president to an “elephant in the china shop.”</p><p>“We share a lot of the same goals. We definitely don't share a style,” the Downers Grove resident said, referring to Trump. “I come from a totally different background. I'm a boring CPA. He's a reality TV show, New York real estate developer … But he's got the hardest job in the world, and I probably have the second hardest job in the world, being chairman of the Illinois Republican Party.”</p><p>Trump has certainly complicated matters for the state party in the suburbs, which provided the lifeblood of the Illinois GOP for generations. Former President Joe Biden won DuPage County by 18 percentage points in 2024.</p><p>Grogan contends the “evolution in the suburbs” started under former President Barack Obama. </p><p>But he acknowledges the headwinds the MAGA movement has brought to suburbs that used to be reliably red.</p><p>“[Trump] brought in blue-collar voters that weren't ours before, and that's a good thing and it's a challenging thing,” Grogan said. “Blue-collar voters need to be enticed a little bit more. They need to be excited a little bit more." </p><p>Grogan doesn’t push Trump’s false conspiracy theory of widespread voter fraud costing him the 2020 presidential election, and Grogan says his party needs to embrace mail voting the president has sowed doubt about.</p><p>But the new chair is quick to note “no system is zero-fraud and zero-error” — including the one in DuPage County that saw him lose his bid for a third term as auditor.</p><p>“In 2020, I lost by 76 votes out of a half a million, and I will tell you that the error rate was probably north of that, because we threw out over 800 ballots,” Grogan said. “People should know that every vote does count, and we want to count every vote accurately.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" alt="Illinois Republican Party chair Bob Grogan, pictured at Chicago Public Media offices. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/79de3c8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2Fff%2F010ada2a4eea933946ed2a7e0479%2Fgrogan-2609020077.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/02f8adc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2Fff%2F010ada2a4eea933946ed2a7e0479%2Fgrogan-2609020077.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/79de3c8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2Fff%2F010ada2a4eea933946ed2a7e0479%2Fgrogan-2609020077.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Illinois Republican Party chair Bob Grogan, pictured at Chicago Public Media offices. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As for abortion rights that remain popular and important to many suburban voters, Grogan, who calls himself pro-life, decried Illinois as “an abortion destination state, and I don't think that's what the average suburban, pro-choice person really wants.</p><p>“They don't want late-term abortions. They don't want taxpayer-funded abortions for folks that aren't even citizens,” Grogan said. “Abortion tourism is not something that they would really endorse.”</p><p>And he’s undaunted by the odds playing on heavily gerrymandered, Democratic-drawn maps.</p><p>“Voter patterns change, and they evolve. I have optimism … that eventually governance matters, and I think that the governance of the state of Illinois, and city of Chicago, leaves a lot to be desired,” Grogan said. “That old definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again, expecting a different result.”</p><p>But Republicans are running Darren Bailey again this November against Gov. JB Pritzker, four years after the southern Illinois farmer got trounced by the billionaire governor who’s now heavily favored to win a third term.</p><p>Grogan backed Ted Dabrowski <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/02/23/illinois-republican-primary-governor-candidates-preview-bailey-dabrowski-heidner-mendrick" target="_blank" ><u>in the GOP primary</u></a> and now says Bailey “has definitely come back at it with a different approach … We have structural problems. But if you only believed polls, Hillary Clinton would be president.”</p><p>More importantly, Grogan said, “There is definitely a lot more JB fatigue than there was six years ago.</p><p>“You bring up the governor's name, and there's a grimace. Where they were giving the benefit of the doubt a couple cycles ago, they're not so happy,” he said, pointing to COVID-19 business restrictions under Pritzker early in the pandemic and the governor’s potential White House ambitions in 2028.</p><p>“A lot of people are getting the impression he's looking over the person's shoulder at New Hampshire, and the recipe for New Hampshire and Iowa is not the recipe for Illinois,” said Grogan, who’s tasked with working up a fundraising rebound, too.</p><p>The Democratic Party of Illinois’ $1.2 million cash on hand at the end of June roughly quadrupled the state GOP’s total. Meanwhile, Bailey entered the summer with about $128,000 in his campaign fund compared to more than $3 million for Pritzker, who can cut another massive check anytime he pleases.</p><p>“We've had an over-reliance on one or two donors on the Republican side, which means that we've been lazy on developing infrastructure for small-dollar donors and such that really should be our bedrock,” Grogan said, referencing the likes of conservative megadonor Richard Uihlein.</p><p>A lot of it will take basic leg work and candidate recruitment. “Even if they aren't going to win someplace, and obviously some ... districts are really hard, I think that a well-crafted dialogue with voters has up-ticket and down-ticket effects,” Grogan said. “The first step is they have to meet us, and then they’ve got to hear us, and then they'll like us. And you can't do that just by listening to the screamers on Facebook.”</p><p>It’s also about changing the mindset of Republicans who “kind of suffer from almost a Stockholm syndrome, that they've been so long outside of power that they no longer identify [with] what it's like … to get power,” Grogan said.</p><p>“So we argue about how many angels dance on the head of a pin, as opposed to how to most advantageously take back a House seat,” he said. “Fratricide is not a great campaign strategy."</p><p>“We are in the super minority, and we've been there for a long time. We haven't held statewide office for quite a few years now. But the same was said 40 years ago — like the governor's mansion was ours exclusively,” Grogan said.</p><p>“There's no magic flipping of a switch … We actually have to not fight about things that aren't really as determinative to the average person trying to make their mortgage payment or their rent payment,” Grogan said. “We have prescriptions for many of the ills. At some point, I think the voters are going to stop digging deeper and look out of the hole that they've dug themselves into.”</p>

entries.title: Review: The young cast of Kokandy Productions’ ‘Hair’ embraces protest as performance with fierce conviction
entries.summary: <p>The new production of the seminal rock musical “Hair” from rapidly rising Kokandy Productions made me remember a famous quote from Yogi Berra: “The future ain't what it used to be.”</p><p>I’ve seen a fair number of productions of “Hair,” which first appeared on Broadway in 1968, but this is the first that’s an expression from a Gen Z-ish point of view. Director Brennan Urbi and his young, game cast embrace the protest-as-performance concept with fierce conviction. In case you miss that point, they’ll indicate it plainly and visibly. “This is a satire,” reads the tie-dyed textile unfurled early and left hanging for the rest of the show’s duration. “This is a protest, not a play,” reads one sign held up during the show’s “be-in.”</p><p>But this isn’t the Age of Aquarius we’re used to. When they talk and sing about anger, injustice and despair, you feel it. But when they talk and sing about love, harmony and understanding, you don’t. They may be wearing flowers, but very few come across as flower children.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘Hair’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8c0000" name="module-8c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Sept. 13<br><b>Where:</b> Chopin Theatre, 1543 W. Division St.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $55.20, $65.87<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.kokandyproductions.com/" target="_blank" >kokandyproductions.com</a><br><b>Run time:</b> 2 hours and 30 minutes with one intermission</div> </div><p>This is a jaded “Hair,” sometimes even a tortured “Hair,” filled with confusion and complexity, with a clear, if underlying, skepticism of the idealism that was a central dimension of the show’s original vibe.</p><p>Urbi’s direction and choreography capture the organic and groovy quality of a show whose style came out of the avant-garde theater of the time, privileging in-the-moment authenticity over narrative. It moves freely and engages with the audience. The band and singing, under the musical direction of Kara Olander, sound strong and confident with Gerome Ragni, James Rado and Galt MacDermot’s famed score, which includes that opening “Age of Aquarius,” “Good Morning Starshine,” “Hair” and many more memorable mainstream hits.</p><p>It’s in the design work and some characterizations where we begin to see our world. The wood risers surrounding the main playing space in Eleanor Kahn’s set, as well as some of the walls, have been graffitied with protest aphorisms, including references to Trump, Palestinians, ICE and even artificial intelligence. Audience members can borrow a marker and add their own during intermission.</p><p>The costuming has flowy dresses and skirts for both men and women, with barely a bell-bottom in sight. We get a Woof (a likable Stone TeSelle) with red/pink in his hair and moustache, and a Hud (charismatic Joshua Emmanuel) clad in leather, neither of which read hippie. The gender fluid costume choices for the ensemble reflect today’s nonconformity to traditional norms, self-consciously comparable to men celebrating long hair.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-510000" name="image-510000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9ffb43e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+148/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fb8%2Fc24a95994ce4986760f4b3219c36%2Fhair-5-photo-by-michael-brosilow.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c663e23/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+148/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fb8%2Fc24a95994ce4986760f4b3219c36%2Fhair-5-photo-by-michael-brosilow.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/08fae6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+148/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fb8%2Fc24a95994ce4986760f4b3219c36%2Fhair-5-photo-by-michael-brosilow.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Hair 5. Photo by Michael Brosilow.jpg" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/08fae6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+148/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fb8%2Fc24a95994ce4986760f4b3219c36%2Fhair-5-photo-by-michael-brosilow.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fc6611e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+148/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fb8%2Fc24a95994ce4986760f4b3219c36%2Fhair-5-photo-by-michael-brosilow.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/08fae6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+148/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fb8%2Fc24a95994ce4986760f4b3219c36%2Fhair-5-photo-by-michael-brosilow.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>(left to right) Zac Richey , Gavin Rhys , Joshua Emmanuel , Diana Marilyn Alvarez and Caitlin Dobbins in Kokandy Productions’ revival of “Hair.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As Berger, a compelling central figure handing out joints and acid tabs, Zac Richey bravely embraces an abrasive, jittery take on the character, less championing freedom than rebelliously rejecting its opposite. Gavin Rhys plays Claude, whose internal battle over whether to burn his draft card provides the show’s dominant throughline, as particularly spaced out from the start. It’s a passive acting choice, but he sounds great singing songs like “Where Do I Go?” and it anticipates his later expressionistic hallucinations. These two form a love triangle with Sheila, played by Catherine Rodriguez O’Connor, who has among the most polished voices, and feels more convincing than others that this “tribe” is trying to transform the world.</p><p>There’s passion here, and commitment, although many of the songs, including O’Connor’s beautiful “Easy to Be Hard,” feel pitched as anthems and targeted into the ether — not the audience, and not their fellow tribe members. These characters feel partial because they don’t seem to have believable relationships with each other.</p><p>Urbi sometimes digs for complexity where simplicity will do, the most egregious example being a confusing “Frank Mills,” with Amy Yeston Kim, who portrays Crissy, summoning the memory from a journal entry.</p><p>This show gets the work’s seriousness, and plumbs its continuing relevancies with great effectiveness, particularly in its fever dream of Act 2 where we see one example after another of imperial destruction.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div And the choice to ditch the nudity and not replace it with anything that feels thematically freeing, seems … well, uptight. Depending on where you’re sitting, the performers will come within inches, but there’s also a carefulness — in our era, people ask permission before contact.</p><p>This isn’t wrong; it’s revealing. This production exalts so much of what “Hair” is about. But I’m not sure it’s aware it is so guarded, earnest, moody and cynical, that when the cast sings the finale, “Let the Sunshine In,” they don’t.</p>

entries.title: Man shot and killed during fight in Lincoln Park, 1 in custody
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot and killed during a fight Sunday night in Lincoln Park on the North Side. </p><p>The 30-year-old man was in a fight around 11:45 p.m. in the 2200 block of North Lincoln Avenue when he was shot multiple times in the body, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to the Illinois Masonic Medical Center where he died, police said. </p><p>A firearm was recovered at the scene, officials said. </p><p>A person was placed into custody and charges were pending. </p>

ride-hailing drivers struggle</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujhrlt-l-o/" target="_blank" >Kade Heather</a></h5><p><b>Taxi troubles</b>: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, major commuting pattern shifts have hurt taxis and ride-hailing services in Chicago. Then there's the emerging threat of autonomous vehicles looming over both. Still, cab drivers have had the roughest road to navigate as the industry evolves.</p><p><b>Cab costs</b>: The competition from ride-hailing apps has sharply reduced the demand for cabs and therefore the value of taxi medallions, the government-issued permits required for taxis. In Chicago, the price of a taxi medallion peaked in 2012 at nearly $400,000, according to city data. Now, they go for about $5,000, which has left many Chicago cabbies in significant debt.</p><p><b>Fare hike</b>: City Council last spring raised cab fares by 20%, the industry's first hike in a decade. A few weeks since the increase went into effect at the start of the month, one driver told the Sun-Times that while they see the hike as "positive" — as long-overdue help to keep up with ride-hailing competition and skyrocketing costs — it may be too late.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujhrlt-l-b/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>WATCH: CAN CHICAGO SAVE TAXIS? ▶️</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/c1F4j_DSZz0?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Can Chicago save its taxis? 5,000 people jump to the same beat. made its official return Saturday, demonstrating a wide range of Black art at the Salt Shed.</p><p>Performers ran the gamut, from Piwa, a young, alternative Zimbabwe artist who sang an unexpected but delightful cover of Betty Davis' 50-year-old funk song "Nasty Gal," to the newly formed Black Opera Ensemble, which belted out  African American spirituals as well as traditional opera selections by Mozart and Bizet.</p><p>Later, the same stage would be graced by the Red Clay Dance Company and legendary rapper Big Daddy Kane.</p><p>Showcasing that diversity of Black talent at an event historically considered a house and hip-hop institution was a goal of its founder, Eric Williams. And it's a major reason why he decided to bring the party back after announcing its end in 2023, after a 20-year run — especially during America's 250th anniversary.</p><p>"It's just reclaiming what being American means," said Williams, 56, who owns the Silver Room boutique in Hyde Park, where he also lives. "If you think about American culture, mostly it's Black culture. The block party has been a celebration of music, art, dance and our contributions to this country."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wujhrlt-l-ii/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's the best way to make a new friend as an adult?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Email your answer to us</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Former Holiday Hills police chief charged with making nearly 300 unauthorized searches: court records
entries.summary: <p>A former Holiday Hills police chief and part-time Prairie Grove officer was charged with making hundreds of unauthorized searches during his time with the departments. </p><p>William Copp, 54, was charged with 12 felony counts of official misconduct, according to McHenry County court records. </p><p>Between February 2024 and November 2025, Copp allegedly used the LEADS network and LEADS data for personal purposes 31 different times while acting in his official capacity as a police officer, prosecutors said. Additionally, he used the Flock ALPR system owned by the Prairie Grove Police Department to make nearly 250 unauthorized searches. </p><p>An arrest warrant for Copp was authorized last month and he resigned from his role as chief of the Holiday Hills police department a short time later, records show. </p><p>During an initial hearing, Copp was ordered released under the conditions he couldn’t contact those he conducted the searches on, go to the Prairie Grove or Holiday Hills police departments other than to pick up his belongings, or own a firearm. </p><p>Additionally, Copp can't work as a police officer while the charges are pending, court records show. </p><p>The pending charges have put the future of the Holiday Hills police department in limbo. </p><p>While the Village Board of Trustees work toward a long-term decision, deputies with the McHenry County sheriff's office were handling all emergency and non-emergency calls through Aug. 31, according to reporting from <a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/northwest-herald/2026/07/18/holiday-hills-police-department-could-be-disbanded-after-chief-charged-with-felony-misconduct/?utm_source=second-street&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=nwhmorningupdate2024&emailmd5=f54c0bb1d245d9928f9c7a3dd6316c25&emailsha1=1812201771865016164239188137254208255249462109823722796&emailsha256=92bd1e9706eb5d69eb208a34b9d2aeb9751e58fd12f6cee70b7ef8d2145fa5f8" target="_blank" >Shaw Local</a>. </p><p>Officials from the McHenry County sheriff's office and Prairie Grove and Holiday Hills police departments didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. </p><p>Copp is expected to appear for an arraignment hearing Wednesday morning. </p>

entries.title: Former Illinois public health chief Nirav Shah drops Maine Senate bid
entries.summary: <p>Illinois' former public health chief who oversaw a series of fatal Legionnaires disease outbreaks at the Quincy veterans home has dropped his bid for the U.S. Senate in Maine — one of several Democrats who are instead supporting the candidacy of Troy Jackson, the state's Senate president. </p><p>Nirav Shah dropped out of the race on Sunday after the Maine Democratic Party held weekend caucuses to determine who would be best to replace Graham Platner as the party’s nominee to take on Maine’s Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. The race is pivotal in determining control of Congress’ upper chamber. Platner dropped out of the state’s U.S. Senate race amid sexual assault allegations, although he has said his decision was not an admission of guilt.</p><p>Shah, who also led Maine's Center for Disease Control and Prevention and served as deputy director for the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said in a statement that Democrats can't defeat Collins "without a united Democratic Party" while endorsing Jackson. Shah most recently lost the primary for governor in Maine. </p><p>"Susan Collins, Donald Trump, and Senate Republicans are banking on disunity and frustration from Maine Democrats to try and win this seat, and we are not going to give them that," Shah said. "Maine Democrats are united, angry, and energized. Now, that energy moves to the most important fight of all: defeating Susan Collins and flipping the United States Senate.”</p><p>Shah joined Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, Dan Kleban, a brewery owner, and Jordan Wood, a former Capitol Hill staffer, in suspending their campaigns over the weekend. Bellows is the only candidate who has not announced an endorsement of Jackson. </p><p>Before moving to Maine, Shah presided over a series of fatal Legionnaires disease outbreaks at the state of Illinois’ veterans’ home in Quincy that were linked to 14 resident deaths and the sickening of dozens of other staff and residents at the former facility. His oversight under Republican Gov. Bruce Rauner’s administration was condemned at the time for worsening the horrific and preventable public health crisis and causing a greater loss of life.</p><p>The debacle, which was laid bare in a series of investigative reports by <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/surviving-war-but-not-the-veterans-home" target="_blank" >WBEZ</a>, helped Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker wrest the Executive Mansion from Rauner in 2018, led to new state laws and a new veterans home in Quincy, and it prompted more than $6 million in wrongful death payouts by the state to victims’ families.</p><p>Some Illinoisans quickly spoke out about Shah's candidacy, including U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, state Sen. Cristina Castro, D-Elgin, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/10/nirav-shah-legionnaires-disease-quincy-veterans-home-maine-senate-bruce-rauner-tim-miller-ilinois-public-health" target="_blank" >Tim Miller, the son of a veteran who died at the downstate Quincy veterans’ home</a> amid the Legionnaires’ disease outbreak.</p><p>Duckworth, who asked for Shah’s resignation in 2018, responded to his candidacy by posting on social media: “Maine deserves better than someone who put his public image before the safety of our veterans. Shah responded that he had "deep respect" for Duckworth but dismissed criticism over his handling of the outbreak at Quincy by calling them "recycled attacks" from "outside groups." </p><p>Shah has addressed the outbreak publicly, most recently at a May 5 Maine gubernatorial primary debate. </p><p>“I could have done better, and that is, as you noted, I could have done a better job communicating, and I learned that lesson,” Shah said.</p><p><i>Contributing: Dave McKinney</i><br></p>

entries.title: Fans de Chicago se reúnen en el parque para ver Argentina contra España en la final de la Copa del Mundo
entries.summary: <p>Tan pronto como Lauren Boyer se enteró de que iba a haber una fiesta para ver la final de la Copa del Mundo en Pilsen, supo que tenía que estar allí. Y todos sus amigos también.</p><p>Estuvieron entre docenas de aficionados al fútbol que se reunieron en el Harrison Park el domingo por la tarde para ver el partido, animando y cubriéndose la boca en los momentos tensos. Algunos incluso levantaron sus propias tarjetas rojas y amarillas —que eran muestras de pintura de una ferretería cercana— en las pocas ocasiones en que la transmisión se interrumpió o cuando no estaban de acuerdo con los árbitros.</p><p>Aunque el juego terminó en lágrimas para Boyer, quien llevaba una camiseta de Lionel Messi —España derrotó a Argentina, ampliando su racha invicta a 38 y continuando una imbatibilidad que se mantiene desde principios de 2024— también hubo algo de alegría. Estaba feliz de haber podido ver el partido junto a sus vecinos y de patear una pelota con desconocidos, aunque eso significaba ver a una de las leyendas más grandes del deporte terminar lo que probablemente fuera su última Copa del Mundo con una derrota.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-590000" Pero este año, sus estudiantes la convencieron de seguir viendo.</p><p>“Me da la oportunidad de conectarme con ellos”, dijo Márquez. “Sólo estoy aquí para disfrutar del juego”.</p><p>Junto al partido había camiones de comida y personas pateando balones de fútbol, así como el exjugador estrella de la MLS, Mike Magee, y Omar González, ex Defensor del Año de la MLS y asistente del <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire" target="_blank" >Chicago Fire FC</a> en el equipo reserva. González, un aficionado de Lamine Yamal, dijo que había estado apoyando a España desde que Estados Unidos y México fueron eliminados.</p><p>Dijo que ver un evento deportivo es, por naturaleza, un evento comunitario, uno que previamente había disfrutado con su familia y compañeros de equipo, por lo que espera ver a Chicago crear más espacios donde los jóvenes puedan reunirse y practicar deportes, ya sea viendo o jugando.</p><p>“Creo que el fútbol es muy similar a la música en el sentido de que une a personas de todas las culturas”, dijo González. “En cada Copa del Mundo recuerdas dónde y con quién estabas...
